subtitulo: Yo invito settles the bill before it becomes a negotiation, and separate checks are one clean sentence if you'd rather split
cena: The bill lands in the middle of the table, four hands reach for it at once, and the fastest hand is the one that actually decides how tonight ends.
decisao: quem paga — quem convida costuma pagar no México, diferente de dividir automaticamente; dividir é possível, mas é uma escolha explícita, não o padrão
frasePiso: The person who invites usually pays. It isn't generosity showing off — it's just who asked.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: In Mexico, splitting the bill is less common than in some other cultures; whoever invites friends or family out is typically expected to pay, though splitting can still be requested explicitly.
fatosDatados.fonte: Consenso de guias culturais (Janine in the World; SpanishStep); norma social, não regra legal

steps.pt: Tonight's decision happens before a drink is ordered: who invited whom. That decides who reaches for the bill later.

steps.es: Vamos por unas cervezas, yo invito.
steps.pt: Let's go for some beers, I'm inviting.
steps.tts: Vamos por unas cervezas, yo invito.

steps.pt: Yo invito isn't an offer to refuse — it's who's paying tonight. The expected answer is thanks, not a fight.

steps.promptPt: A friend says he's inviting. Accept it plainly, with thanks. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you very much, that's kind of you.
You're allowed to want the other arrangement — splitting isn't the default, so say so early, before the tab runs.

steps.promptPt: You'd rather split the bill this time. Say so, before ordering. Speak now.

steps.pt: One more version, for a group sharing a table but not a tab: everyone pays for what they actually had.

steps.promptPt: Suggest that everyone pays for their own order. Speak now.
steps.pt: Each person pays for their own.
Leaving before the rest of the table doesn't need a speech — one line covers the exit.

steps.promptPt: You're heading out while the others stay. Say goodbye to the table. Speak now.
steps.es: Ya me voy. Gracias por todo, nos vemos.

steps.pt: I'm heading out. Thanks for everything, see you.
steps.tts: Ya me voy. Gracias por todo, nos vemos.

steps.promptPt: You are the one who invited. Ask for it first. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh dah lah KWEN-tah por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Can I have the bill, please?

steps.promptPt: They paid last time. Claim your turn. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can I be the one to invite this time?

steps.promptPt: Check before adding your own. Speak now.
Ask the server to do the splitting. Speak now.

aprofundar.titulo: Who pays is a decision, not an accident

secoes.titulo: Yo invito is not a bid to be refused
secoes.corpo: In many English-speaking cultures, an offer to pay gets a ritual refusal first. In this context, yo invito is closer to a plain announcement — the graceful response is thanks, not insistence on paying your share.

secoes.titulo: Splitting is a request, not the default
secoes.corpo: Asking to split is completely normal and many places accommodate it easily — it just isn't assumed the way it might be elsewhere, so naming it early avoids confusion when the bill actually arrives.

secoes.titulo: Leaving a table doesn't require a production
secoes.corpo: Ya me voy plus a short thanks is a complete, socially smooth exit from a group that's staying longer. There's no expectation of a formal round of goodbyes.

permissao: You are allowed to let someone else pay without a fight over the bill. Accepting yo invito gracefully is not freeloading — trying to force a split against someone's clear invitation is the move that actually causes friction here.
espelho: The instinct to reach for your wallet and insist on paying your share the moment someone says 'I've got this' is a very English-speaking reflex — plenty of cultures worldwide expect you to simply say thank you, and this is one of them.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A friend says 'yo invito' before you've even sat down, and your instinct is to insist you'll pay for your own drinks, or to try to split it later anyway.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I don't want to be a burden, or it's only polite to insist on paying my share.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Whoever extends the invitation typically expects to pay — it's less about generosity as performance and more about who initiated the outing. Repeatedly insisting on paying your share can actually read as rejecting the gesture rather than as politeness.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Accept plainly with muchas gracias, and if you want to return the favour, invite them out yourself another time.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The evening stays warm and simple instead of turning into a small tug-of-war over the bill.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when the group explicitly organizes the outing together with no single host — in that case, asking ¿podemos pagar por separado? upfront is the completely normal move.
